In this retrospective series of 33 patients with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity treated with high-dose oral vitamin D, symptom relief was reported in 26 of 30 patients with available symptom data (87%). Anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33 patients (73%). Thirty patients also received concurrent supportive therapy. No treatment-related adverse events were reported. Post-treatment vitamin D levels were measured in only 13 patients; other laboratory data were inconsistently available.

These results support the feasibility of administering high-dose vitamin D alongside ongoing anticancer therapy without apparent interruption, and they document observed symptom improvement in the majority of assessed patients. However, the uncontrolled design, lack of an untreated comparison group, absence of patient-level outcome pairing, and incomplete laboratory follow-up prevent causal attribution of recovery to vitamin D. The safety claim is limited by the small sample, selective adverse-event reporting, and missing post-treatment calcium, renal function, and vitamin D levels in most patients. Concurrent supportive therapy further confounds attribution. The data generate hypotheses but do not establish efficacy or general safety; formal prospective controlled study is warranted.
